claim: Photoreceptor degeneration is a major cause of blindness and a considerable health burden during aging.
source: Photoreceptor degeneration is a major cause of blindness and a considerable health burden during aging but effective therapeutic or preventive strategies have not so far become readily available.
evidence: This is a general statement about the clinical significance of photoreceptor degeneration, drawing from established medical knowledge.

claim: Effective therapeutic or preventive strategies for photoreceptor degeneration have not become readily available.
source: Photoreceptor degeneration is a major cause of blindness and a considerable health burden during aging but effective therapeutic or preventive strategies have not so far become readily available.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of clinical treatment options, based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: KIT signaling protects photoreceptor cells against light-induced retinal degeneration in mouse models.
source: Here, we show in mouse models that signaling through the tyrosine kinase receptor KIT protects photoreceptor cells against both light-induced and inherited retinal degeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including ERG measurements, histological analysis, and TUNEL assays.

claim: KIT signaling protects photoreceptor cells against inherited retinal degeneration in mouse models.
source: Here, we show in mouse models that signaling through the tyrosine kinase receptor KIT protects photoreceptor cells against both light-induced and inherited retinal degeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from rd10 and rd1 mouse models presented in Figure 9 and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Photoreceptor cells upregulate Kit ligand (KITL) upon light damage.
source: Upon light damage, photoreceptor cells upregulate Kit ligand (KITL) and activate KIT signaling, which in turn induces nuclear accumulation of the transcription factor NRF2 and stimulates the expression of the antioxidant gene Hmox1.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data, RT-PCR, western blots, and immunostaining shown in Figure 1.

claim: Light damage activates KIT signaling in photoreceptor cells.
source: Upon light damage, photoreceptor cells upregulate Kit ligand (KITL) and activate KIT signaling, which in turn induces nuclear accumulation of the transcription factor NRF2 and stimulates the expression of the antioxidant gene Hmox1.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data showing increased phosphorylated KIT in Figure 1G,H.

claim: KIT signaling induces nuclear accumulation of the transcription factor NRF2.
source: Upon light damage, photoreceptor cells upregulate Kit ligand (KITL) and activate KIT signaling, which in turn induces nuclear accumulation of the transcription factor NRF2 and stimulates the expression of the antioxidant gene Hmox1.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and western blot data in Figure 7 showing increased nuclear NRF2 in Kit+/+ but not KitWps/Wps mice after light damage.

claim: KIT signaling stimulates the expression of the antioxidant gene Hmox1.
source: Upon light damage, photoreceptor cells upregulate Kit ligand (KITL) and activate KIT signaling, which in turn induces nuclear accumulation of the transcription factor NRF2 and stimulates the expression of the antioxidant gene Hmox1.
evidence: This is supported by western blot and immunostaining data in Figure 6 showing increased HMOX1 expression in Kit+/+ but not KitWps/Wps retinas after light damage.

claim: A viable Kit mutation promotes light-induced photoreceptor damage.
source: Conversely, a viable Kit mutation promotes light-induced photoreceptor damage, which is reversed by experimental expression of Hmox1.
evidence: This is supported by ERG measurements, histological analysis, and TUNEL assays in Figure 3 showing greater damage in KitWps/Wps mice compared to Kit+/+ mice after light exposure.

claim: Light-induced photoreceptor damage in Kit mutant mice is reversed by experimental expression of Hmox1.
source: Conversely, a viable Kit mutation promotes light-induced photoreceptor damage, which is reversed by experimental expression of Hmox1.
evidence: This is supported by ERG measurements and histological analysis in Figure 8 showing that AAV8-HMOX1 partially rescues retinal function and structure in KitWps/Wps albino mice after light damage.

claim: Overexpression of KITL from a viral AAV8 vector prevents photoreceptor cell death after light damage.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of KITL from a viral AAV8 vector prevents photoreceptor cell death and partially restores retinal function after light damage or in genetic models of human retinitis pigmentosa.
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assays and histological analysis in Figure 4 showing reduced photoreceptor cell death in AAV8-KITL infected retinas after light damage.

claim: Overexpression of KITL from a viral AAV8 vector partially restores retinal function after light damage.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of KITL from a viral AAV8 vector prevents photoreceptor cell death and partially restores retinal function after light damage or in genetic models of human retinitis pigmentosa.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the prevention of photoreceptor cell death and structural preservation shown in Figure 4, though direct ERG measurements after AAV8-KITL treatment in light-damaged mice are not explicitly shown in the abstract context.

claim: Overexpression of KITL from a viral AAV8 vector prevents photoreceptor cell death in genetic models of human retinitis pigmentosa.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of KITL from a viral AAV8 vector prevents photoreceptor cell death and partially restores retinal function after light damage or in genetic models of human retinitis pigmentosa.
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assays in Figure 9 and Figure 9—figure supplement 1 showing reduced photoreceptor cell death in rd10 and rd1 mice infected with AAV8-KITL.

claim: Overexpression of KITL from a viral AAV8 vector partially restores retinal function in genetic models of human retinitis pigmentosa.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of KITL from a viral AAV8 vector prevents photoreceptor cell death and partially restores retinal function after light damage or in genetic models of human retinitis pigmentosa.
evidence: This is supported by ERG measurements in Figure 9F,G and Figure 9—figure supplement 1B showing improved b-wave amplitudes in rd10 and rd1 mice infected with AAV8-KITL.

claim: Application of KITL may provide a novel therapeutic avenue for prevention or treatment of retinal degenerative diseases.
source: Hence, application of KITL may provide a novel therapeutic avenue for prevention or treatment of retinal degenerative diseases.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental data showing protective effects of KITL in mouse models.

claim: Photoreceptor loss is common to cone dystrophy, retinitis pigmentosa (RP), and age-related macular degeneration (AMD).
source: Such photoreceptor cell loss is common to a number of degenerative eye disorders including cone dystrophy, retinitis pigmentosa (RP) and the highly prevalent age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Ma et al., 2019; Mitchell et al., 2018; Wright et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RP has been associated with mutations in about 80 genes.
source: RP, for instance, has been associated with mutations in about 80 genes and can be inherited as an autosomal-dominant, autosomal-recessive, or X-linked trait (Dias et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: RP can be inherited as an autosomal-dominant, autosomal-recessive, or X-linked trait.
source: RP, for instance, has been associated with mutations in about 80 genes and can be inherited as an autosomal-dominant, autosomal-recessive, or X-linked trait (Dias et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: RP is characterized initially by degeneration of rod photoreceptors, followed by a loss of cone photoreceptors and of the photoreceptor-trophic retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).
source: It is characterized initially by degeneration of rod photoreceptors, followed by a loss of cone photoreceptors and of the photoreceptor-trophic retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).
evidence: This statement describes the pathological progression of RP based on established knowledge.

claim: RP patients suffer from progressive night blindness, tunnel vision and, rarely, may become totally blind.
source: Consequently, patients suffer from progressive night blindness, tunnel vision and, rarely, may become totally blind (Dias et al., 2018; Hartong et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Gene therapy has recently been approved for a specific causative mutation (RPE65).
source: Although gene therapy has recently been approved for a specific causative mutation (RPE65) (Russell et al., 2017), there are still no broadly applicable and efficacious treatments available to prevent or cure vision loss caused by photoreceptor degeneration.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: There are still no broadly applicable and efficacious treatments available to prevent or cure vision loss caused by photoreceptor degeneration.
source: Although gene therapy has recently been approved for a specific causative mutation (RPE65) (Russell et al., 2017), there are still no broadly applicable and efficacious treatments available to prevent or cure vision loss caused by photoreceptor degeneration.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of clinical treatment options, based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Several neuroprotective factors have been identified based on results obtained with transgenic and conditional knockout animals and pharmacological treatments.
source: In fact, several neuroprotective factors have been identified based on results obtained with transgenic and conditional knockout animals and pharmacological treatments (Joly et al., 2008; Ueki et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Neuroprotective factors include ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF), glial cell–derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF), pigment epithelium-derived factor (PEDF) and rod-derived cone viability factor (RdCVF).
source: They include ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF), glial cell–derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF), pigment epithelium-derived factor (PEDF) and rod-derived cone viability factor (RdCVF), all of which might potentially be used to treat photoreceptor degeneration in humans (Aït-Ali et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2019; Del Río et al., 2011; Wen et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Clinical application of neuroprotective factors is hampered by relatively short half-lives, systemic side effects and reduced efficacy.
source: Their clinical application, however, is hampered by relatively short half-lives, systemic side effects and reduced efficacy, and none are commercially available for clinical use (Pardue and Allen, 2018; Scholl et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: None of the identified neuroprotective factors are commercially available for clinical use.
source: Their clinical application, however, is hampered by relatively short half-lives, systemic side effects and reduced efficacy, and none are commercially available for clinical use (Pardue and Allen, 2018; Scholl et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Limited light stress activates the FGF2/gp130 signaling pathway.
source: It is known that limited light stress activates the FGF2/gp130 signaling pathway (Liu et al., 1998; Ueki et al., 2009) and that prolonged exposure to light upregulates CNTF and FGF2, although usually at levels too low to protect against retinal degeneration (LaVail et al., 1998; Wen et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Prolonged exposure to light upregulates CNTF and FGF2, although usually at levels too low to protect against retinal degeneration.
source: It is known that limited light stress activates the FGF2/gp130 signaling pathway (Liu et al., 1998; Ueki et al., 2009) and that prolonged exposure to light upregulates CNTF and FGF2, although usually at levels too low to protect against retinal degeneration (LaVail et al., 1998; Wen et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Excessive light may play a role in worsening genetically influenced retinal degenerations such as AMD.
source: That LD is a valid strategy to identify novel retinoprotective factors is underscored by the role excessive light may play in worsening genetically influenced retinal degenerations such as AMD (Organisciak and Vaughan, 2010; Suzuki et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: KITL (also known as stem cell factor, SCF, or mast cell growth factor, MGF) stimulates an important signaling pathway by interacting with its receptor, KIT.
source: One of them is Kit ligand (Kitl) whose protein product, KITL (also known as stem cell factor, SCF, or mast cell growth factor, MGF), stimulates an important signaling pathway by interacting with its receptor, KIT (also known as the proto-oncogene c-KIT) and promotes cell survival, migration and proliferation (Hou and Pavan, 2008; Lennartsson and Rönnstrand, 2012; Li and Hou, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: KITL promotes cell survival, migration and proliferation.
source: One of them is Kit ligand (Kitl) whose protein product, KITL (also known as stem cell factor, SCF, or mast cell growth factor, MGF), stimulates an important signaling pathway by interacting with its receptor, KIT (also known as the proto-oncogene c-KIT) and promotes cell survival, migration and proliferation (Hou and Pavan, 2008; Lennartsson and Rönnstrand, 2012; Li and Hou, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: KIT is a multi-domain transmembrane tyrosine kinase expressed in a variety of cell types including melanocytes, germ cells and cells of the hematopoietic lineage.
source: KIT is a multi-domain transmembrane tyrosine kinase expressed in a variety of cell types including melanocytes, germ cells and cells of the hematopoietic lineage, and is required for their normal development and function (Blume-Jensen et al., 2000; Comazzetto et al., 2019; Hou et al., 2000; Yuzawa et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: KIT is required for normal development and function of melanocytes, germ cells and cells of the hematopoietic lineage.
source: KIT is a multi-domain transmembrane tyrosine kinase expressed in a variety of cell types including melanocytes, germ cells and cells of the hematopoietic lineage, and is required for their normal development and function (Blume-Jensen et al., 2000; Comazzetto et al., 2019; Hou et al., 2000; Yuzawa et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Interaction of KIT with its ligand leads to receptor dimerization and autophosphorylation.
source: Interaction of KIT with its ligand leads to receptor dimerization and autophosphorylation which in turn activates the MAPK pathway, phosphatidylinositol 3'-kinase (PI3K), JAK/STAT and SRC family members (Hou and Pavan, 2008; Lennartsson and Rönnstrand, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: KIT receptor dimerization and autophosphorylation activates the MAPK pathway, phosphatidylinositol 3'-kinase (PI3K), JAK/STAT and SRC family members.
source: Interaction of KIT with its ligand leads to receptor dimerization and autophosphorylation which in turn activates the MAPK pathway, phosphatidylinositol 3'-kinase (PI3K), JAK/STAT and SRC family members (Hou and Pavan, 2008; Lennartsson and Rönnstrand, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in Kit cause severe anemia, pigmentation abnormalities, sterility, mast cell deficits, spatial learning memory deficits and defects in peripheral nerve regeneration in mice.
source: In mice, loss-of-function mutations in Kit cause severe anemia, pigmentation abnormalities, sterility, mast cell deficits, spatial learning memory deficits and defects in peripheral nerve regeneration (Gore et al., 2008; Motro et al., 1996; Wen et al., 2010; Zsebo et al., 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: KIT has been found to be expressed in retinal progenitor cells.
source: Nevertheless, although KIT has been found to be expressed in retinal progenitor cells (Koso et al., 2007; Zou et al., 2019), its functional role in the adult retina is still unknown.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The functional role of KIT in the adult retina is still unknown.
source: Nevertheless, although KIT has been found to be expressed in retinal progenitor cells (Koso et al., 2007; Zou et al., 2019), its functional role in the adult retina is still unknown.
evidence: This statement reflects the state of knowledge prior to the current study.

claim: Mice homozygous for the KitWps mutation show an exacerbated photoreceptor degeneration after light damage.
source: Here, we find that mice homozygous for the KitWps mutation (Guo et al., 2010) show an exacerbated photoreceptor degeneration and that overexpression of KITL can prevent photoreceptor cell death in light-damaged mice.
evidence: This is supported by ERG measurements, histological analysis, and TUNEL assays in Figure 3.

claim: Overexpression of KITL can prevent photoreceptor cell death in light-damaged mice.
source: Here, we find that mice homozygous for the KitWps mutation (Guo et al., 2010) show an exacerbated photoreceptor degeneration and that overexpression of KITL can prevent photoreceptor cell death in light-damaged mice.
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assays and histological analysis in Figure 4.

claim: KIT signaling stimulates the expression of Hmox1 in an NRF2-dependent manner.
source: Furthermore, we show that KIT signaling stimulates the expression of Hmox1 in an NRF2-dependent manner and that experimental expression of Hmox1 in KitWps homozygotes prevents light-induced photoreceptor degeneration.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7 showing that knockdown of Nfe2l2 blocks KIT-induced upregulation of Hmox1.

claim: Experimental expression of Hmox1 in KitWps homozygotes prevents light-induced photoreceptor degeneration.
source: Furthermore, we show that KIT signaling stimulates the expression of Hmox1 in an NRF2-dependent manner and that experimental expression of Hmox1 in KitWps homozygotes prevents light-induced photoreceptor degeneration.
evidence: This is supported by ERG measurements and histological analysis in Figure 8.

claim: After 1 day of continuous light exposure (15,000 Lux), BALB/c neural retinas showed no obvious signs of retinal degeneration, but increased expression of GFAP.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, after 1 day of continuous exposure (15,000 Lux), BALB/c neural retinas showed no obvious signs of retinal degeneration, but increased expression of GFAP.
evidence: This is supported by histological images and GFAP immunostaining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: After three days of continuous light exposure (15,000 Lux), there was significant retinal degeneration in BALB/c mice.
source: After three days of continuous exposure, however, there was significant retinal degeneration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A to C).
evidence: This is supported by histological images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A to C.

claim: RNA-seq analysis identified a large number of genes whose expression was significantly changed in LD-treated neural retinas compared with non-treated ones.
source: The RNA-seq data showed a large number of genes whose expression was significantly changed (p adjust value <0.01 and fold change >2) in the LD-treated neural retinas compared with the non-treated ones (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the volcano plot shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Light damage induces expression of known light-inducible genes such as Gfap, Edn2, Fgf2, Ccl3 and Ccl12.
source: These genes included known light-inducible ones such as Gfap, Edn2, Fgf2, Ccl3 and Ccl12 (Figure 1B) and hence supported the validity of this approach (Hadziahmetovic et al., 2012; Rattner and Nathans, 2005; Rutar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the heat map in Figure 1B and citations to previous literature.

claim: KEGG analysis identified the MAPK pathway among the top 20 altered signaling pathways after light damage.
source: A KEGG (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes) analysis identified the MAPK pathway among the top 20 altered signaling pathways (Figure 1C), with increased expression, for instance, of the genes encoding LIF, KITL and NGF (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the KEGG analysis bar graph shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Light damage increases expression of genes encoding LIF, KITL and NGF.
source: A KEGG (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes) analysis identified the MAPK pathway among the top 20 altered signaling pathways (Figure 1C), with increased expression, for instance, of the genes encoding LIF, KITL and NGF (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the heat map shown in Figure 1D.

claim: RT-PCR confirmed differential expression of Kitl, Lif, and Ngf identified by RNA-seq analysis.
source: RT-PCR confirmed their differential expression identified by the RNA-seq analysis. In particular, Kitl expression was significantly increased in the neural retina after LD (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Both mature transmembrane and cleaved soluble forms of KITL (45 and 19 kDa, respectively) were increased after light damage.
source: Quantitation of western blot bands showed that both mature transmembrane and cleaved soluble forms of KITL (45 and 19 kDa, respectively) were increased (m-KITL, 2.4 ± 0.9 fold; s-KITL, 4.5 ± 1.6 fold; n = 5) (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Phosphorylated KIT was increased after light damage, although not total KIT.
source: Phosphorylated KIT (indicative of activated KIT), although not total KIT, was also increased (3.14 ± 0.94, n = 5) (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1G,H.

claim: Upregulation of KITL was predominantly seen in photoreceptor inner segments after light damage.
source: Immunostaining showed that upregulation of KITL was predominantly seen in photoreceptor inner segments (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Kitl expression is higher in the neural retina compared to RPE under normal light conditions.
source: Quantitative PCR data showed higher Kitl expression in the neural retina (14.6 ± 7.2 fold, n = 3) compared to RPE (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Q-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Upon light damage, Kitl was upregulated in neural retinas but hardly in RPE.
source: Furthermore, upon LD, Kitl was upregulated in neural retinas (6.7 ± 1.2 fold compared to normal light condition, n = 3) but hardly in RPE (1.24 ± 0.36 fold compared to normal light condition, n = 3) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by Q-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: Under normal light conditions, the level of KITL protein was 5.11 ± 0.29 fold higher in the photoreceptor tissue compared to RPE.
source: Western blot data showed that under normal light conditions, the level of KITL protein was 5.11 ± 0.29 fold higher in the photoreceptor tissue compared to RPE (based on three independent samples) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,C.

claim: In situ hybridization showed that light stress significantly increased the Kitl signal in photoreceptor cells but not in RPE cells.
source: These results were supported by in situ hybridization (ISH), showing that light stress significantly increased the Kitl signal in photoreceptor cells but not in RPE cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Photoreceptor cells rather than RPE cells are the major source of increased Kitl expression following light stress.
source: Hence, the data suggest that photoreceptor cells rather than RPE cells are the major source of increased Kitl expression following light stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the Q-PCR, western blot, and in situ hybridization data showing higher Kitl expression in photoreceptor cells compared to RPE cells.

claim: KitWps homozygotes are viable, although they are totally white and infertile.
source: This allele encodes a KIT protein with an Asp-to-Asn (D-to-N) mutation at residue 60 in the extracellular domain that reduces, but does not completely eliminate, KIT signaling. Consequently, KitWps homozygotes are viable, although they are totally white and infertile (Guo et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: KitWps homozygotes have no detectable changes in fundus.
source: Nevertheless, KitWps homozygotes have no detectable changes in fundus, such as blood vessels and the pigmentation, similar to other point mutations in Kit (Aoki et al., 2009; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by fundus images shown in Figure 2A and a citation to previous literature.

claim: The amplitudes of the a- and b-waves under scotopic or photopic conditions are not significantly different between Kit+/+ and KitWps/Wps mice.
source: Moreover, the amplitudes of the a- and b-waves under scotopic or photopic conditions are not significantly different between Kit+/+ and KitWps/Wps mice (Figure 2B,C), and KitWps/Wps retinas appear structurally intact (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by ERG traces and quantification shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: KitWps/Wps retinas appear structurally intact under normal conditions.
source: Moreover, the amplitudes of the a- and b-waves under scotopic or photopic conditions are not significantly different between Kit+/+ and KitWps/Wps mice (Figure 2B,C), and KitWps/Wps retinas appear structurally intact (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by histological images shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The numbers of cell nuclei in the ganglion cell layer (GCL), inner nuclear layer (INL) and outer nuclear layer (ONL) were similar between Kit+/+ and KitWps/Wps retinas.
source: Also, the numbers of cell nuclei in the ganglion cell layer (GCL), inner nuclear layer (INL) and outer nuclear layer (ONL) were similar to those in Kit+/+ retinas (Figure 2E) and immunoreactivities for markers for bipolar cells (OTX2), 'On' bipolar cells (PKCα), rod photoreceptor cells (Rhodopsin) and cone photoreceptor cells (Opsin) were as in Kit+/+ retinas (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Immunoreactivities for markers for bipolar cells (OTX2), 'On' bipolar cells (PKCα), rod photoreceptor cells (Rhodopsin) and cone photoreceptor cells (Opsin) were similar between Kit+/+ and KitWps/Wps retinas.
source: Also, the numbers of cell nuclei in the ganglion cell layer (GCL), inner nuclear layer (INL) and outer nuclear layer (ONL) were similar to those in Kit+/+ retinas (Figure 2E) and immunoreactivities for markers for bipolar cells (OTX2), 'On' bipolar cells (PKCα), rod photoreceptor cells (Rhodopsin) and cone photoreceptor cells (Opsin) were as in Kit+/+ retinas (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images shown in Figure 2F.

claim: There was no significant difference in the number of bipolar cells and cone photoreceptor cells between Kit+/+ and KitWps/Wps retinas.
source: Likewise, there was also no significant difference in the number of bipolar cells and cone photoreceptor cells (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Under normal conditions, the KitWps mutation does not cause detectable changes in retinal function, histology, or structure.
source: These data show that under normal conditions, the KitWps mutation does not cause detectable changes in retinal function, histology, or structure.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the ERG, histological, and immunostaining data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Western blots and immunostaining using the AB5506 antibody did not detect differences in KIT expression levels between Kit+/+ and KitWps homozygous retinas.
source: As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, western blots and immunostaining using the AB5506 antibody (recognizing the intracellular kinase domain of KIT) did not detect differences in KIT expression levels between Kit+/+ and KitWps homozygous retinas.
evidence: This is supported by western blot and immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Immunostaining using the ACK45 antibody showed a significantly decreased immunoreactivity in the photoreceptor layer, the inner plexiform layer and the ganglion cell layer of KitWps/Wps retinas.
source: However, immunostaining using the ACK45 antibody (recognizing the extracellular immunoglobulin domain of wild type, although not Wps/Wps KIT protein) showed a significantly decreased immunoreactivity in the photoreceptor layer, the inner plexiform layer and the ganglion cell layer of KitWps/Wps retinas (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Upon intravitreal injection of KITL, phosphorylation of KIT and its downstream targets ERK and AKT were prominent in Kit+/+ but not in KitWps/Wps retinas.
source: Indeed, upon intravitreal injection of KITL, phosphorylation of KIT and its downstream targets ERK and AKT were prominent in Kit+/+ but not in KitWps/Wps retinas (Figure 2I,J).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2I,J.

claim: The KitWps mutation substantially reduced activation of KIT by KITL in the neural retina.
source: These results indicate that the mutation substantially reduced activation of KIT by KITL in the neural retina.
evidence: This is inferred from the western blot data showing reduced phosphorylation of KIT, ERK, and AKT in KitWps/Wps retinas after KITL injection.

claim: C57BL/6J mice express the Leu450-Met variant of RPE65 and show reduced susceptibility to light damage.
source: Even though C57BL/6J mice express the Leu450-Met variant of RPE65 and show reduced susceptibility to LD (Wenzel et al., 2001), they have been used as a suitable model of light-induce retinal damage (LIRD) because their susceptibility to LD is similar to that of humans (Ding et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: C57BL/6J mice have been used as a suitable model of light-induced retinal damage (LIRD) because their susceptibility to LD is similar to that of humans.
source: Even though C57BL/6J mice express the Leu450-Met variant of RPE65 and show reduced susceptibility to LD (Wenzel et al., 2001), they have been used as a suitable model of light-induce retinal damage (LIRD) because their susceptibility to LD is similar to that of humans (Ding et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: After light damage, the a- and b-wave amplitudes declined more in KitWps/Wps mice compared to Kit+/+ mice under scotopic conditions.
source: After LD, the a- and b-wave amplitudes declined in Kit+/+ to 294 ± 37μV and 521 ± 27μV, respectively (n = 8) and in KitWps/Wps mice to 188 ± 80μV and 365 ± 63μV, respectively (n = 8). These data indicate that the rod-driven circuit was damaged more severely in KitWps/Wps retinas compared to Kit+/+ retinas.
evidence: This is supported by ERG measurements shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: The rod-driven circuit was damaged more severely in KitWps/Wps retinas compared to Kit+/+ retinas after light damage.
source: After LD, the a- and b-wave amplitudes declined in Kit+/+ to 294 ± 37μV and 521 ± 27μV, respectively (n = 8) and in KitWps/Wps mice to 188 ± 80μV and 365 ± 63μV, respectively (n = 8). These data indicate that the rod-driven circuit was damaged more severely in KitWps/Wps retinas compared to Kit+/+ retinas.
evidence: This is inferred from the ERG measurements showing greater decline in a- and b-wave amplitudes in KitWps/Wps mice.

claim: Under photopic conditions, the b-wave ERG responses were weakened in KitWps/Wps mice more severely than those in Kit+/+ mice after light damage.
source: Similarly, under photopic conditions (cone response) (Figure 3B,D), the b-wave ERG responses were weakened in KitWps/Wps mice more severely (from 89.4 ± 15μV to 40 ± 10μV, n = 8) than those in Kit+/+ mice (from 95 ± 13μV to 61 ± 9μV, n = 8), indicating that the cone-driven circuit was also damaged more severely in KitWps/Wps retinas.
evidence: This is supported by ERG measurements shown in Figure 3B,D.

claim: The cone-driven circuit was damaged more severely in KitWps/Wps retinas compared to Kit+/+ retinas after light damage.
source: Similarly, under photopic conditions (cone response) (Figure 3B,D), the b-wave ERG responses were weakened in KitWps/Wps mice more severely (from 89.4 ± 15μV to 40 ± 10μV, n = 8) than those in Kit+/+ mice (from 95 ± 13μV to 61 ± 9μV, n = 8), indicating that the cone-driven circuit was also damaged more severely in KitWps/Wps retinas.
evidence: This is inferred from the ERG measurements showing greater decline in b-wave amplitudes in KitWps/Wps mice under photopic conditions.

claim: Normal KIT signaling helps to protect against retinal damage following light damage.
source: These results suggest that normal KIT signaling helps to protect against retinal damage following LD.
evidence: This is inferred from the ERG data showing greater functional impairment in KitWps/Wps mice compared to Kit+/+ mice after light damage.

claim: Light-damaged KitWps/Wps retinas showed a severely reduced thickness of the ONL both in superior and inferior regions compared to light-damaged Kit+/+ retinas.
source: As shown in Figure 3E, compared to light-damaged Kit+/+ retinas, similarly treated KitWps/Wps retinas showed a severely reduced thickness of the ONL both in superior and inferior regions (Figure 3E, panels a, F).
evidence: This is supported by histological images and quantification shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: After light stress, Müller glial cells became positive for GFAP, but much more so in KitWps/Wps compared to Kit+/+ mice.
source: In unstressed Kit+/+ or mutant retinas, GFAP immunoreactivity, indicative of reactive gliosis, was only detected in the ganglion cell layer, while after light stress, Müller glial cells also became positive for GFAP, but much more so in KitWps/Wps compared to Kit+/+ mice (Figure 3E, panels b).
evidence: This is supported by GFAP immunostaining images shown in Figure 3E, panels b.

claim: Rhodopsin immunoreactivity was more severely reduced in light-damaged KitWps/Wps compared to Kit+/+ retinas and showed abnormal presence in the ONL.
source: Likewise, Rhodopsin immunoreactivity was not only more severely reduced in light-damaged KitWps/Wps compared to Kit+/+ retinas but also showed abnormal presence in the ONL (Figure 3E, arrows in panels c).
evidence: This is supported by Rhodopsin immunostaining images shown in Figure 3E, panels c.

claim: The number of dead cells in the ONL was much higher in KitWps/Wps retinas (44 ± 9, n = 10) compared to Kit+/+ retinas (22 ± 7 per section, n = 10) after light damage.
source: As shown in Figure 3E (panels D) and 3G, although dead cells were present in the ONL of Kit+/+ retinas (22 ± 7 per section, n = 10), their number was much higher in KitWps/Wps retinas (44 ± 9, n = 10).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay images and quantification shown in Figure 3E,G.

claim: After excessive light exposure, the photoreceptor cells of KitWps/Wps mice are structurally and functionally impaired to a greater extent than those of Kit+/+ mice.
source: Hence, these data show that after excessive light exposure, the photoreceptor cells of KitWps/Wps mice are not only structurally but also functionally impaired to a greater extent than those of Kit+/+ mice.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the ERG, histological, and TUNEL data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The KitWps mutation accelerates photoreceptor degeneration during light damage.
source: The findings indicate that the KitWps mutation accelerates photoreceptor degeneration during LD.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing greater structural and functional impairment in KitWps/Wps mice compared to Kit+/+ mice after light damage.

claim: Fourteen days after AAV8-CMV-GFP virus infection, GFP was found in nearly the entire retina.
source: Fourteen days after virus infection, fundus photographs showed that GFP was found in nearly the entire retina, and cross-sections showed strong GFP signals in photoreceptor cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by fundus photographs and cross-section images shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cross-sections showed strong GFP signals in photoreceptor cells fourteen days after AAV8-CMV-GFP virus infection.
source: Fourteen days after virus infection, fundus photographs showed that GFP was found in nearly the entire retina, and cross-sections showed strong GFP signals in photoreceptor cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by cross-section images shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Two weeks after AAV8-KITL infection, western blots showed a significantly increased expression of KITL (3.3 ± 0.46 fold over uninjected control, n = 4).
source: Two weeks after infection, we isolated the neural retinas and examined them for KITL expression. Western blots showed a significantly increased expression of KITL (3.3 ± 0.46 fold over uninjected control, n = 4) (Figure 4B), and immunostaining showed that overexpression of KITL was almost entirely restricted to photoreceptors in the retinas (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Overexpression of KITL was almost entirely restricted to photoreceptors in the retinas after AAV8-KITL infection.
source: Two weeks after infection, we isolated the neural retinas and examined them for KITL expression. Western blots showed a significantly increased expression of KITL (3.3 ± 0.46 fold over uninjected control, n = 4) (Figure 4B), and immunostaining showed that overexpression of KITL was almost entirely restricted to photoreceptors in the retinas (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Without light damage, neither AAV8 nor AAV8-KITL caused detectable changes of retinal morphology in albino mice.
source: Without LD, neither AAV8 (schematically shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A) nor AAV8-KITL caused detectable changes of retinal morphology in these mice (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is supported by histological images shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: After 3 days of light damage treatment, retinas infected by AAV8-KITL were thicker than those infected by control AAV8 or left uninfected.
source: After 3 days of LD treatment, retinas infected by AAV8-KITL were thicker than those infected by control AAV8 or left uninfected (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is supported by histological images and quantification shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: Infection with AAV8 control or AAV8-KITL virus did not cause photoreceptor cell death under normal light conditions.
source: Furthermore, TUNEL analysis showed that infection with AAV8 control or AAV8-KITL virus did not cause photoreceptor cell death under normal light conditions, but under LD conditions, photoreceptor cell death was less pronounced when AAV8-KITL was used (9 ± 1.6%, n = 6) compared to when control AAV8 was used (40.8 ± 4.5%, n = 6) or the eyes were left uninfected (37.7 ± 5%, n = 6) (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay images and quantification shown in Figure 4F,G.

claim: Under light damage conditions, photoreceptor cell death was less pronounced when AAV8-KITL was used (9 ± 1.6%, n = 6) compared to when control AAV8 was used (40.8 ± 4.5%, n = 6) or the eyes were left uninfected (37.7 ± 5%, n = 6).
source: Furthermore, TUNEL analysis showed that infection with AAV8 control or AAV8-KITL virus did not cause photoreceptor cell death under normal light conditions, but under LD conditions, photoreceptor cell death was less pronounced when AAV8-KITL was used (9 ± 1.6%, n = 6) compared to when control AAV8 was used (40.8 ± 4.5%, n = 6) or the eyes were left uninfected (37.7 ± 5%, n = 6) (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay images and quantification shown in Figure 4F,G.

claim: Overexpression of KITL prevents light-induced photoreceptor degeneration in Kit wild type mice.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that overexpression of KITL prevents light-induced photoreceptor degeneration in Kit wild type mice.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the histological and TUNEL data presented in Figure 4.

claim: After 3 days of light damage treatment, the retinas in both Kit+/+ albino and KitWps/Wps albino mice showed reduced thickness and near-absence of outer segments, but the effects were more severe in KitWps/Wps albino compared with Kit+/+ albino mice.
source: After 3 days of LD treatment, the retinas in both Kit+/+ albino and KitWps/Wps albino mice showed reduced thickness and near-absence of outer segments, but the effects were more severe in KitWps/Wps albino compared with Kit+/+ albino mice (Figure 4H,I).
evidence: This is supported by histological images and quantification shown in Figure 4H,I.

claim: Injection of the AAV8-KITL virus prevented light-induced reduction of retinal thickness in Kit+/+ albino mice but not in KitWps/Wps albino mice.
source: Importantly, injection of the AAV8-KITL virus prevented light-induced reduction of retinal thickness in Kit+/+ albino mice but not in KitWps/Wps albino mice (Figure 4H,I).
evidence: This is supported by histological images and quantification shown in Figure 4H,I.

claim: TUNEL assays showed a cell death rate of 40.6 ± 8.2% in Kit+/+ albino mice and 78 ± 11.4% in KitWps/Wps albino mice (n = 4) after control infection.
source: Consistent with these results, TUNEL assays showed a cell death rate of 40.6 ± 8.2% in Kit+/+ albino mice and 78 ± 11.4% in KitWps/Wps albino mice (n = 4) after control infection, while infection with AAV8-KITL significantly reduced the death rate of photoreceptor cells to 8.9 ± 2.1% in Kit+/+ albino mice but not in KitWps/Wps albino mice, where it remained high (75.9 ± 8.2%, n = 4) (Figure 4H,J).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay images and quantification shown in Figure 4H,J.

claim: Infection with AAV8-KITL significantly reduced the death rate of photoreceptor cells to 8.9 ± 2.1% in Kit+/+ albino mice but not in KitWps/Wps albino mice, where it remained high (75.9 ± 8.2%, n = 4).
source: Consistent with these results, TUNEL assays showed a cell death rate of 40.6 ± 8.2% in Kit+/+ albino mice and 78 ± 11.4% in KitWps/Wps albino mice (n = 4) after control infection, while infection with AAV8-KITL significantly reduced the death rate of photoreceptor cells to 8.9 ± 2.1% in Kit+/+ albino mice but not in KitWps/Wps albino mice, where it remained high (75.9 ± 8.2%, n = 4) (Figure 4H,J).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay images and quantification shown in Figure 4H,J.

claim: Overexpression of KITL can prevent photoreceptor cell death from light damage through activation of the receptor KIT.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that overexpression of KITL can prevent photoreceptor cell death from LD through activation of the receptor KIT.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that AAV8-KITL protects Kit+/+ but not KitWps/Wps mice from light-induced photoreceptor cell death.

claim: At 2 weeks after injection of AAV8-RPE65-KITL, overexpression of KITL was prominent in the RPE (12.1 ± 2.4 fold, n = 4).
source: As shown in Figure 5C and D, at 2 weeks after injection of AAV8-RPE65-KITL, overexpression of KITL was prominent in the RPE (12.1 ± 2.4 fold, n = 4), but its protective effect against LD was very limited (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Overexpression of KITL in RPE has a very limited protective effect against light damage.
source: As shown in Figure 5C and D, at 2 weeks after injection of AAV8-RPE65-KITL, overexpression of KITL was prominent in the RPE (12.1 ± 2.4 fold, n = 4), but its protective effect against LD was very limited (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is supported by histological images and quantification shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: The death rate of photoreceptor cells was 26.6 ± 5%, n = 8 after infection with AAV8-RPE65-Flag and only slightly reduced to 21.7 ± 2.8%, n = 8 after infection with AAV8-RPE65-KITL.
source: In fact, the death rate of photoreceptor cells was 26.6 ± 5%, n = 8 after infection with AAV8-RPE65-Flag and only slightly reduced to 21.7 ± 2.8%, n = 8 after infection with AAV8-RPE65-KITL (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-a and B).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay images and quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-a and B.

claim: Overexpression of KITL in RPE does not play a major role in prevention of light-induced photoreceptor degeneration.
source: Hence, overexpression of KITL in RPE does not play a major role in prevention of light-induced photoreceptor degeneration.
evidence: This is inferred from the TUNEL data showing only a slight reduction in photoreceptor cell death after AAV8-RPE65-KITL infection.

claim: Infection with AAV8-RHO-KITL led to overexpression specifically in photoreceptor cells (increase over control by 4.23 ± 0.68 fold, n = 4).
source: Infection with AAV8-RHO-KITL led to overexpression specifically in photoreceptor cells as shown by WB (increase over control by 4.23 ± 0.68 fold, n = 4) and IF (Figure 5G and H), confirming previous reports (Allocca et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by western blot and immunostaining data shown in Figure 5G,H and a citation to previous literature.

claim: Overexpression of KITL in photoreceptor cells reduced the light damage-induced decrease of ONL thickness.
source: In contrast to overexpression in RPE, however, overexpression of KITL in photoreceptor cells reduced the LD-induced decrease of ONL thickness (Figure 5I,J) and prevented photoreceptor cell death (from 25.9 ± 4.7%, n = 8 after infection with AAV8-RHO-Flag to 11.5 ± 2.5%, n = 8 after infection with AAV8-RHO-KITL (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-b, C).
evidence: This is supported by histological images and quantification shown in Figure 5I,J.

claim: Overexpression of KITL in photoreceptor cells prevented photoreceptor cell death (from 25.9 ± 4.7%, n = 8 after infection with AAV8-RHO-Flag to 11.5 ± 2.5%, n = 8 after infection with AAV8-RHO-KITL).
source: In contrast to overexpression in RPE, however, overexpression of KITL in photoreceptor cells reduced the LD-induced decrease of ONL thickness (Figure 5I,J) and prevented photoreceptor cell death (from 25.9 ± 4.7%, n = 8 after infection with AAV8-RHO-Flag to 11.5 ± 2.5%, n = 8 after infection with AAV8-RHO-KITL (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-b, C).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay images and quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-b, C.

claim: Overexpression of KITL in photoreceptor cells protects these cells more efficiently than overexpression in RPE cells.
source: Collectively, these results clearly indicate that overexpression of KITL in photoreceptor cells protects these cells more efficiently than overexpression in RPE cells, underscoring the cell-autonomous effect of KITL.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of protective effects between AAV8-RPE65-KITL and AAV8-RHO-KITL.

claim: After light damage, the expression of 17 antioxidant and wound healing genes, including Axl and Hmox1, was changed in Kit+/+ retinas.
source: In fact, after LD, the expression of 17 such genes, including Axl and Hmox1, was changed in Kit+/+ retinas (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by the heat map shown in Figure 6B.

claim: HMOX1 catalyzes the degradation of heme into three biologically active end products, biliverdin/bilirubin, CO and ferrous ion.
source: The protein product of Hmox1, HMOX1, catalyzes the degradation of heme into three biologically active end products, biliverdin/bilirubin, CO and ferrous ion (Otterbein et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: HMOX1 is known to be induced by oxidative stress in multiple tissues as well as by light damage of the retina.
source: It is known to be induced by oxidative stress in multiple tissues as well as by LD of the retina (Kutty et al., 1995) and thought to act as an antioxidant (Otterbein et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HMOX1 is thought to act as an antioxidant.
source: It is known to be induced by oxidative stress in multiple tissues as well as by LD of the retina (Kutty et al., 1995) and thought to act as an antioxidant (Otterbein et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Under normal light/dark cycle conditions, HMOX1 levels were similarly low in both Kit+/+ and KitWps/Wps retinas.
source: Under normal light/dark cycle conditions, HMOX1 levels analyzed on western blots (Figure 6C) or by immunostaining (Figure 6D) were similarly low in both Kit+/+ and KitWps/Wps retinas.
evidence: This is supported by western blot and immunostaining data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: After light damage, HMOX1 expression was significantly upregulated in Kit+/+ retinas (3.6 ± 0.6 fold) but only slightly in KitWps/Wps retinas (1.4 ± 0.5 fold, n = 3).
source: After LD, however, HMOX1 expression was significantly upregulated in Kit+/+ retinas (3.6 ± 0.6 fold) but only slightly in KitWps/Wps retinas (1.4 ± 0.5 fold, n = 3) (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot and immunostaining data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Light damage-dependent upregulation of Hmox1 is markedly influenced by KIT signaling.
source: These data indicate that LD-dependent upregulation of Hmox1 is markedly influenced by KIT signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing differential HMOX1 upregulation between Kit+/+ and KitWps/Wps retinas after light damage.

claim: Transfection with KIT led to upregulation of HMOX1, with a clear difference between KIT-WT (6.2 ± 0.86 fold, n = 4) and KIT-Wps (3 ± 0.6 fold, n = 4) in 661W cells.
source: Transfection with KIT also led to upregulation of HMOX1, although with a clear difference between KIT-WT (6.2 ± 0.86 fold, n = 4) and KIT-Wps (3 ± 0.6 fold, n = 4).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: One week after injection of AAV8-KITL, western blots showed a correlation between high levels of KITL (4.6 ± 0.9 fold induction, n = 4) and HMOX1 (2.9 ± 0.5 fold induction, n = 4) in Kit+/+ mice kept under normal light conditions.
source: One week after injection, western blots showed a correlation between high levels of KITL (4.6 ± 0.9 fold induction, n = 4) and HMOX1 (2.9 ± 0.5 fold induction, n = 4) (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Immunostaining showed that the expression of KITL was dramatically enhanced in the superior retinal region around the location of injection, coinciding with high level HMOX1 expression.
source: Consistent with this observation, immunostaining showed that the expression of KITL was dramatically enhanced in the superior retinal region around the location of injection, coinciding with high level HMOX1 expression (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Activation of KIT signaling can induce HMOX1 expression in Kit+/+ retinas independent of light damage treatment.
source: These data suggest that activation of KIT signaling can induce HMOX1 expression in Kit+/+ retinas independent of LD treatment.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing increased HMOX1 expression after AAV8-KITL injection in mice kept under normal light conditions.

claim: Western blots showed no change in NRF2 expression in retinas after light treatment.
source: Although western blots showed no change in NRF2 expression in retinas after light treatment (Figure 7A,B), immunostaining indicated a dramatic increase in nuclear accumulation of NRF2 in photoreceptor cells after light treatment for 8 days (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Immunostaining indicated a dramatic increase in nuclear accumulation of NRF2 in photoreceptor cells after light treatment for 8 days.
source: Although western blots showed no change in NRF2 expression in retinas after light treatment (Figure 7A,B), immunostaining indicated a dramatic increase in nuclear accumulation of NRF2 in photoreceptor cells after light treatment for 8 days (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Nuclear accumulation of NRF2 was much reduced in KitWps/Wps mice (14 ± 5 per section, n = 6) compared to Kit+/+ mice (28 ± 9, n = 6) after light treatment.
source: This nuclear accumulation was much reduced in KitWps/Wps mice (14 ± 5 per section, n = 6) compared to Kit+/+ mice (28 ± 9, n = 6) (Figure 7C,D), suggesting that Kit signaling regulates nuclear translocation of NRF2 in photoreceptor cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images and quantification shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: Kit signaling regulates nuclear translocation of NRF2 in photoreceptor cells.
source: This nuclear accumulation was much reduced in KitWps/Wps mice (14 ± 5 per section, n = 6) compared to Kit+/+ mice (28 ± 9, n = 6) (Figure 7C,D), suggesting that Kit signaling regulates nuclear translocation of NRF2 in photoreceptor cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing differential nuclear accumulation of NRF2 between Kit+/+ and KitWps/Wps mice after light treatment.

claim: Knockdown of Kitl increased the number of 661W cells with cytosolic NRF2 expression from 4.74 ± 2.27% to 30.2 ± 8.3% or 36.8 ± 2.24% (n = 3).
source: Indeed, immunostaining revealed that both Kitl-si-RNAs increased the number of cells with cytosolic NRF2 expression from 4.74 ± 2.27% to 30.2 ± 8.3% or 36.8 ± 2.24% (n = 3), respectively (Figure 7E,F).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images and quantification shown in Figure 7E,F.

claim: Knock down of Kitl increased the levels of NRF2 in the cytoplasm (1.5 ± 0.13 fold, n = 3) and decreased the levels of nuclear NRF2 (0.59 ± 0.09 fold, n = 3) in 661W cells.
source: In addition, western blots showed that knock down of Kitl increased the levels of NRF2 in the cytoplasm (1.5 ± 0.13 fold, n = 3) and decreased the levels of nuclear NRF2 (0.59 ± 0.09 fold, n = 3) (Figure 7G,H).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7G,H.

claim: KIT signaling regulates the cytoplasmic/nuclear distribution of NRF2 in photoreceptor cells.
source: Taken together, these data clearly show that KIT signaling regulates the cytoplasmic/nuclear distribution of NRF2 in photoreceptor cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the immunostaining and western blot data showing effects of Kitl knockdown on NRF2 localization.

claim: Overexpression of KIT upregulated Hmox1 expression (2.35 ± 1 fold, n = 3) in 661W cells.
source: Consistently, overexpression of KIT did not significantly change Nfe2l2 expression (1.1 ± 0.2 fold, n = 3) but upregulated Hmox1 expression (2.35 ± 1 fold, n = 3). This upregulation was blocked by knockdown of Nfe2l2.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR and qPCR data shown in Figure 7I,J.

claim: Upregulation of Hmox1 by overexpression of KIT was blocked by knockdown of Nfe2l2 in 661W cells.
source: Consistently, overexpression of KIT did not significantly change Nfe2l2 expression (1.1 ± 0.2 fold, n = 3) but upregulated Hmox1 expression (2.35 ± 1 fold, n = 3). This upregulation was blocked by knockdown of Nfe2l2.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR and qPCR data shown in Figure 7I,J.

claim: KIT signaling activates NRF2 to regulate the expression of Hmox1 in photoreceptor cells.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that KIT signaling activates NRF2 to regulate the expression of Hmox1 in photoreceptor cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data showing that knockdown of Nfe2l2 blocks KIT-induced upregulation of Hmox1.

claim: Western blotting and immunostaining showed photoreceptor-restricted expression of HMOX1 two weeks after AAV8-HMOX1 virus infection.
source: Western blotting and immunostaining showed photoreceptor-restricted expression after 2 weeks after virus infection (Figure 8A,B), with levels similar to those observed in uninjected Kit+/+ retinas after LD.
evidence: This is supported by western blot and immunostaining data shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: Without light damage, control AAV8 or AAV8-HMOX1 virus did not cause significant changes in the ERG scotopic trace in KitWps/Wps albino mice.
source: ERG measurements showed that without LD, control AAV8 or AAV8-HMOX1 virus did not cause significant changes in the ERG scotopic trace (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This is supported by ERG traces shown in Figure 8C,D.

claim: Following 3 days of light damage, the b-wave amplitudes were higher when AAV8-HMOX1 was used (381 ± 40μV, n = 5) compared to when control AAV8 was used (152 ± 33 μV, n = 5) in KitWps/Wps albino mice.
source: Following 3 days of LD, however, the amplitudes of ERG scotopic traces were depressed after infection with AAV8 or AAV8-HMOX1 virus, but the b-wave amplitudes were higher when AAV8-HMOX1 was used (381 ± 40μV, n = 5) compared to when control AAV8 was used (152 ± 33 μV, n = 5) (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This is supported by ERG traces and quantification shown in Figure 8C,D.

claim: Overexpression of HMOX1 partially rescues retinal function in the KitWps/Wps albino mice during light damage.
source: These results suggest that overexpression of HMOX1 partially rescues retinal function in the KitWps/Wps albino mice during LD.
evidence: This is inferred from the ERG data showing improved b-wave amplitudes in AAV8-HMOX1 infected mice compared to control.

claim: After light damage, AAV8-HMOX1-infected retinas were thicker than control AAV8-infected ones, especially with respect to the photoreceptor cell layer.
source: Furthermore, histological analyses showed that after LD, AAV8-HMOX1-infected retinas were thicker than control AAV8-infected ones, especially with respect to the photoreceptor cell layer (Figure 8E,F).
evidence: This is supported by histological images and quantification shown in Figure 8E,F.

claim: Overexpression of HMOX1 protects photoreceptor cells in KitWps/Wps albino retinas against light damage.
source: These data suggest that overexpression of HMOX1 protects photoreceptor cells in KitWps/Wps albino retinas against LD and that LD-induced HMOX1 plays an important antioxidant role in retinas in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the histological data showing increased retinal thickness in AAV8-HMOX1 infected mice after light damage.

claim: Light damage-induced HMOX1 plays an important antioxidant role in retinas in vivo.
source: These data suggest that overexpression of HMOX1 protects photoreceptor cells in KitWps/Wps albino retinas against LD and that LD-induced HMOX1 plays an important antioxidant role in retinas in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the protective effects of HMOX1 overexpression against light damage.

claim: Addition of exogenous KITL (5.6 nM) was able to prevent cell loss caused by light damage in 661W cells (from 409 ± 44 to 147 ± 15 (n = 3) after 8 hr of LD treatment to 278 ± 28 (n = 3)).
source: As shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C and D, cell numbers were similar in each group before LD but dramatically decreased in the control group (from 409 ± 44 to 147 ± 15 (n = 3) after 8 hr of LD treatment). Addition of exogenous KITL (5.6 nM) was able to prevent cell loss caused by LD to 278 ± 28 (n = 3). This preventive effect was totally blocked by knockdown of Hmox1 via Hmox1-si-RNAs (cell loss 147 ± 16, n = 3 and 131 ± 17, n = 3, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: The preventive effect of KITL on light-induced cell loss was totally blocked by knockdown of Hmox1 via Hmox1-si-RNAs in 661W cells.
source: As shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C and D, cell numbers were similar in each group before LD but dramatically decreased in the control group (from 409 ± 44 to 147 ± 15 (n = 3) after 8 hr of LD treatment). Addition of exogenous KITL (5.6 nM) was able to prevent cell loss caused by LD to 278 ± 28 (n = 3). This preventive effect was totally blocked by knockdown of Hmox1 via Hmox1-si-RNAs (cell loss 147 ± 16, n = 3 and 131 ± 17, n = 3, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Stimulation of KITL decreased light-induced cell death rate from 83 ± 4.6% to 40 ± 5.3% (n = 3) in 661W cells, but this protection by KITL disappeared when the expression of Hmox1 was knocked down by Hmox1-si-RNAs.
source: In addition, the data of propidium iodide (PI) staining also showed that stimulation of KITL decreased light-induced cell death rate from 83 ± 4.6% to 40 ± 5.3% (n = 3), but this protection by KITL disappeared when the expression of Hmox1 was knocked down by Hmox1-si-RNAs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by PI staining data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Protection of KITL against light-induced photoreceptor cell loss depends on HMOX1.
source: These results suggest that protection of KITL against light-induced photoreceptor cell loss depends on HMOX1.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that knockdown of Hmox1 blocks the protective effect of KITL in 661W cells.

claim: Mice homozygous for a mutation in the gene encoding the photoreceptor cGMP phosphodiesterase, Pde6brd10, share many characteristics of human retinal degeneration resulting from a mutation in the homologous gene.
source: Mice homozygous for a mutation in the gene encoding the photoreceptor cGMP phosphodiesterase, Pde6brd10 (hereafter called rd10/rd10) share many characteristics of human retinal degeneration resulting from a mutation in the homologous gene (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Subretinal injection of AAV8-KITL virus at P3 can mediate overexpression of KITL in photoreceptor cells of rd10/rd10 mice.
source: As shown in Figure 9A, ectopic expression of KITL was observed at 3 weeks in rd10/rd10 photoreceptor cells in the eye infected with AAV8-KITL, but not in those of the control-injected contralateral eye. These results suggest that subretinal injection of AAV8-KITL virus at P3 can mediate overexpression of KITL in photoreceptor cells of rd10/rd10 mice.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining images shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The thickness of the ONL was significantly increased from the peripheral region to the central region after infection with the AAV8-KITL virus in rd10/rd10 mice.
source: The thickness of the ONL was significantly increased from the peripheral region to the central region after infection with the AAV8-KITL virus (Figure 9B,C).
evidence: This is supported by histological images and quantification shown in Figure 9B,C.

claim: In P24 control-injected rd10/rd10 retina, Rhodopsin was abnormally translocated from the OS to the ONL, a phenomenon that was partially rescued by infection with the AAV8-KITL virus.
source: In P24 control-injected rd10/rd10 retina, Rhodopsin was abnormally translocated from the OS to the ONL, a phenomenon that was partially rescued by infection with the AAV8-KITL virus (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is supported by Rhodopsin immunostaining images shown in Figure 9D.

claim: TUNEL analysis showed a large number of dead cells in the ONL of rd10/rd10 mice infected with control AAV8 virus (death rate, 16.2 ± 2%, n = 5), but a significantly reduced number after AAV8-KITL virus infection (8.9 ± 1.6%, n = 5).
source: TUNEL analysis showed a large number of dead cells in the ONL of rd10/rd10 mice infected with control AAV8 virus (death rate, 16.2 ± 2%, n = 5), but a significantly reduced number after AAV8-KITL virus infection (8.9 ± 1.6%, n = 5) (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay images and quantification shown in Figure 9E.

claim: The ERG analysis revealed that the scotopic traces of control eyes presented nearly horizontal lines (b-wave amplitude, 142.2 ± 43.60.4μV, n = 5), while infection with the AAV8-KITL virus led to clear a- and b-waves (b-wave amplitude, 304 ± 30μV, n = 5) in rd10/rd10 mice.
source: The ERG analysis revealed that the scotopic traces of control eyes presented nearly horizontal lines (b-wave amplitude, 142.2 ± 43.60.4μV, n = 5), while infection with the AAV8-KITLvirus led to clear a- and b-waves (b-wave amplitude, 304 ± 30μV, n = 5) (Figure 9F,G), suggesting that overexpression of KITL partially restores the retinal function in rd10/rd10 mice.
evidence: This is supported by ERG traces and quantification shown in Figure 9F,G.

claim: Overexpression of KITL partially restores the retinal function in rd10/rd10 mice.
source: The ERG analysis revealed that the scotopic traces of control eyes presented nearly horizontal lines (b-wave amplitude, 142.2 ± 43.60.4μV, n = 5), while infection with the AAV8-KITLvirus led to clear a- and b-waves (b-wave amplitude, 304 ± 30μV, n = 5) (Figure 9F,G), suggesting that overexpression of KITL partially restores the retinal function in rd10/rd10 mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the ERG data showing improved a- and b-wave amplitudes in AAV8-KITL infected rd10/rd10 mice.

claim: Overexpression of KITL prevents photoreceptor cell death and partially restores retinal function not only in light damage but also genetic models of retinal degeneration.
source: Taken together, these results strongly indicate that overexpression of KITL prevents photoreceptor cell death and partially restores retinal function not only in LD but also genetic models of retinal degeneration.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data from rd10 and rd1 mouse models presented in Figure 9 and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Activation of KIT signaling in photoreceptor cells activates NRF2, in turn inducing expression of HMOX1, and protects these cells against light-induced degeneration.
source: Several lines of evidence support the notion that activation of KIT signaling in photoreceptor cells activates NRF2, in turn inducing expression of HMOX1, and protects these cells against light-induced degeneration.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on multiple lines of experimental evidence presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: KIT is expressed in mouse retina, including in its photoreceptor cells.
source: First, KIT is expressed in mouse retina, including in its photoreceptor cells, and its activation leads to stimulation of the MAPK and the PI3K/AKT pathways.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2H and western blot data in Figure 2I,J.

claim: KIT activation leads to stimulation of the MAPK and the PI3K/AKT pathways.
source: First, KIT is expressed in mouse retina, including in its photoreceptor cells, and its activation leads to stimulation of the MAPK and the PI3K/AKT pathways.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 2I,J showing phosphorylation of ERK and AKT after KITL injection.

claim: The use of KITL and activation of KIT signaling may add to the arsenal of endogenous pathways that may be considered clinically for photoreceptor protection during retinal degeneration.
source: Given these findings, the use of KITL and activation of KIT signaling may add to the arsenal of endogenous pathways that may be considered clinically for photoreceptor protection during retinal degeneration.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The application of endogenous neuroprotective factors would seem to provide a more straightforward therapeutic avenue, with the added benefit that it may work regardless of the actual pathogenetic mechanism underlying photoreceptor degradation.
source: Indeed, in contrast to other strategies such as stem cell therapies, optogenetics and retinal prostheses, which all face major technical and financial investments (Scholl et al., 2016), the application of endogenous neuroprotective factors would seem to provide a more straightforward therapeutic avenue, with the added benefit that it may work regardless of the actual pathogenetic mechanism underlying photoreceptor degradation (Pardue and Allen, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and represents a speculative conclusion.

claim: AAV-mediated expression of neurotrophic factors or antioxidant genes such as RdCVF and NRF2 has proved beneficial in protecting photoreceptors.
source: AAV-mediated expression of neurotrophic factors or antioxidant genes such as RdCVF and NRF2 has indeed proved beneficial in protecting photoreceptors (Leveillard and Sahel, 2010; Liang et al., 2017 Xiong et al., 2015), and similar strategies using KIT activation may prove equally valuable.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Kit signaling can have both beneficial and deleterious effects.
source: Previous studies have indicated, however, that Kit signaling can have both beneficial and deleterious effects (Lennartsson and Rönnstrand, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: KIT is needed for cell development and survival.
source: On the one hand, KIT is needed for cell development and survival (Blume-Jensen et al., 2000; Hou et al., 2000; Wen et al., 2010), but on the other hand, excessive KIT signaling, associated, for instance, with activating KIT mutations, may also lead to formation of tumors, in particular gastrointestinal stromal tumors, adult acute myeloid leukemia, and melanoma (Lennartsson and Rönnstrand, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Excessive KIT signaling may lead to formation of tumors, in particular gastrointestinal stromal tumors, adult acute myeloid leukemia, and melanoma.
source: On the one hand, KIT is needed for cell development and survival (Blume-Jensen et al., 2000; Hou et al., 2000; Wen et al., 2010), but on the other hand, excessive KIT signaling, associated, for instance, with activating KIT mutations, may also lead to formation of tumors, in particular gastrointestinal stromal tumors, adult acute myeloid leukemia, and melanoma (Lennartsson and Rönnstrand, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Activation of KIT signaling should be used with caution in clinical settings.
source: Hence, activation of KIT signaling should be used with caution in clinical settings.
evidence: This is a speculative recommendation based on the known potential for KIT signaling to cause tumors.

claim: Local expression of KITL following intraocular injection of recombinant AAV might considerably reduce potential deleterious effects because gene expression is locally restricted and transfer of protein to other tissues is effectively blocked by the blood retinal barrier.
source: Nevertheless, local expression of KITL following intraocular injection of recombinant AAV might considerably reduce potential deleterious effects because gene expression is locally restricted and transfer of protein to other tissues is effectively blocked by the blood retinal barrier.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on knowledge of AAV-mediated gene delivery and the blood retinal barrier.

claim: It is KITL activation in photoreceptor cells themselves, rather than in RPE cells or potentially other retinal cells, that has protective effects on retinal degeneration.
source: In the current paper we have so far shown that it is KITL activation in photoreceptor cells themselves, rather than in RPE cells or potentially other retinal cells, that has protective effects on retinal degeneration, and that it is cell-autonomous KITL action that protects photoreceptor cells against degeneration.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 showing differential protective effects of AAV8-RPE65-KITL versus AAV8-RHO-KITL.

claim: It is cell-autonomous KITL action that protects photoreceptor cells against degeneration.
source: In the current paper we have so far shown that it is KITL activation in photoreceptor cells themselves, rather than in RPE cells or potentially other retinal cells, that has protective effects on retinal degeneration, and that it is cell-autonomous KITL action that protects photoreceptor cells against degeneration.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 showing that photoreceptor-specific expression of KITL is more protective than RPE-specific expression.

claim: Müller glial cells have been reported to participate in reactive gliosis and regulate retinal repair during retinal injury.
source: Among them are Müller glial cells, which have been reported to participate in reactive gliosis and regulate retinal repair during retinal injury (Too et al., 2017; Goldman, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The pathway downstream of KIT involves a cytoplasm-to-nuclear shift of the transcription factor NRF2, which is likely mediated by KIT signaling-dependent activation of AKT.
source: We have also shown that the pathway downstream of KIT involves a cytoplasm-to-nuclear shift of the transcription factor NRF2, which is likely mediated by KIT signaling-dependent activation of AKT (Yoo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7 and a citation to previous literature.

claim: HMOX1 can reduce oxidative stress by breaking down heme and reducing molecular oxygen and oxygen radicals in the heme oxygenase reaction pathway.
source: The involvement of HMOX1 seems particularly interesting as it can reduce oxidative stress by breaking down heme and reducing molecular oxygen and oxygen radicals in the heme oxygenase reaction pathway (Otterbein et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Photoreceptor cells have a rich complement of mitochondria to accommodate their high metabolic rate and are more sensitive to oxidative stress than many other cell types.
source: Photoreceptor cells have a rich complement of mitochondria to accommodate their high metabolic rate and are more sensitive to oxidative stress than many other cell types (Campochiaro and Mir, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The development of AMD is tightly linked to oxidative damage.
source: The development of AMD, for instance, is tightly linked to oxidative damage (Mitchell et al., 2018), and antioxidant therapy can delay cell loss in retinal degenerative diseases and lead to reduced photoreceptor cell death in experimental animals (Donovan et al., 2001; Haruta et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Antioxidant therapy can delay cell loss in retinal degenerative diseases and lead to reduced photoreceptor cell death in experimental animals.
source: The development of AMD, for instance, is tightly linked to oxidative damage (Mitchell et al., 2018), and antioxidant therapy can delay cell loss in retinal degenerative diseases and lead to reduced photoreceptor cell death in experimental animals (Donovan et al., 2001; Haruta et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Oxidative stress has been observed in many neurodegenerative conditions, including light-induced retinal damage.
source: Oxidative stress has also been observed in many other neurodegenerative conditions, including LIRD, and antioxidant treatment is useful in their prevention (Donovan et al., 2001; Suzuki et al., 2012; Xiong et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Antioxidant treatment is useful in the prevention of neurodegenerative conditions including light-induced retinal damage.
source: Oxidative stress has also been observed in many other neurodegenerative conditions, including LIRD, and antioxidant treatment is useful in their prevention (Donovan et al., 2001; Suzuki et al., 2012; Xiong et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The induction of Hmox1 following light damage can be seen as a homeostatic mechanism operating in photoreceptor cells.
source: The induction of Hmox1 following LD (Hadziahmetovic et al., 2012) can therefore be seen as a homeostatic mechanism operating in photoreceptor cells (Sun et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: KITL overexpression or isolated overexpression of HMOX1 did not lead to full protection against light damage.
source: Nevertheless, it is important to recognize that in our model, KITL overexpression or isolated overexpression of HMOX1 did not lead to full protection against LD.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data showing partial but not complete protection in the various experiments.

claim: The KITL-KIT-NRF2-HMOX1 axis is likely only one among many pathways involved in protection of photoreceptor cells against light damage.
source: Hence, the KITL-KIT-NRF2-HMOX1 axis that we here identified is likely only one among many pathways involved in protection of photoreceptor cells against LD.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that KITL or HMOX1 overexpression provides only partial protection.

claim: The findings provide strong evidence for KIT signaling in protecting photoreceptor cells against light-induced retinal damage as well as against inherited forms of retinal degeneration.
source: In summary, our findings provide strong evidence for KIT signaling in protecting photoreceptor cells against light-induced retinal damage as well as against inherited forms of retinal degeneration.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The findings justify a detailed exploration of how the KIT signaling pathway could be harnessed pharmacologically for prevention or delay of progressive photoreceptor cell and vision loss as seen in AMD, RP and other retinal degenerations.
source: We believe that these findings justify a detailed exploration of how this signaling pathway could be harnessed pharmacologically for prevention or delay of progressive photoreceptor cell and vision loss as seen in AMD, RP and other retinal degenerations.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The findings have implications not only for our understanding of the relationship between genetic and environmental factors in retinal degeneration in general but also as a potential treatment for photoreceptor loss in humans.
source: Hence, the findings have implications not only for our understanding of the relationship between genetic and environmental factors in retinal degeneration in general but also as a potential treatment for photoreceptor loss in humans.
